newsitem.title: JAPAN: Legacy of Lima crisis stress may haunt hostages.
newsitem.headline: Legacy of Lima crisis stress may haunt hostages.

text.p: Many of the Japanese hostages returning home from the siege in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima may face recurring stress from the ordeal, mental health experts said on Thursday.

Psychotherapist Naho Kikuchi said the legacy of 126 days confinement inside the residence, living with the fear of imminent death, will plague some hostages with phantom aches and pains and recurring fears triggered by chance events.

"The symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) are they will feel psychologically stressed without knowing the reason why. For example, on an anniversary date two years from now, they may have a stomach ache and that is a physical sign saying they have to deal with their emotional problem," she said.
Health Counselling Centre director Mariko Kobayashi said the hostages may find themselves transferred to different posts because they are no longer capable of fulfilling their previous duties.

"People who have been working at the highest levels and who suddenly find themselves living in a situation where they don't know if there will be a tomorrow will be carrying a doleful pain with them back to their companies. This will likely have an effect on the position they will be given once they return," she said.
Post-traumatic stress syndrome became a widely known phenomenon in Japan after the 1995 Kobe earthquake and the Tokyo subway sarin nerve gas attack.
In a sign of the government's concerns, the Health Ministry is sending two specialists in mental disorders to Peru.
During the siege, International Red Cross doctors said the 72 hostages were suffering from high blood pressure, mild depression and other stress-related diseases.
However, the mental effects of the siege may outlast the physical deterioration, Kikuchi said.
"Physically they might look OK but psychologically they may be suffering," she said.
The anniversaries of the start of the siege and the storming of the residence may act as triggers for bouts of anguish, Kikuchi added.
"It can get to the point where they can't function, they can't get out of bed and they can't go to work and their relationships start suffering because they're under stress," Kikuchi said.
"They start yelling at their family and it can get very serious."
The inexplicable emotional turmoil PTSD sufferers feel will be particularly hard for the 24 Japanese hostages, who were a glittering array of diplomats and top executives, Kikuchi said.

"The hostages were Japanese men in high positions and...they are told not to express their fear. It's really important for the family members of these men to receive support in dealing with this incident," she said.

Sounds similar to explosions or the martial music blasted on loudspeakers by Peruvian anti-terror troops to mask the sound of tunnels being dug in preparation for storming the compound may also haunt PTSD victims, she said.
"They might look OK but when there's a sound or music that reminds them of the incident...they won't be OK," she said.
The deaths of all 14 of the MRTA guerrillas, many still in their teens, may also leave its mark on the hostages, she said.
